Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arthur Vance had been driving home from the winter assembly when the intersection light turned yellow. The delivery truck had blown through the red, and the screech of tires was followed by a sharp, metallic collapse that seemed to swallow the air itself. Glass rained across the dashboard, the steering column buckled, and for a long moment, there was only the hiss of steam and the ragged pull of his own breath. He remembered stepping out into the damp street, hands trembling, unable to find the right words to describe the tangle of metal, the way the victim’s jacket had caught on a cracked headlight, or how the first responders shouted over the engine noise. Some things simply refused to be spoken. Six months later, Arthur sat in his principal’s office, the afternoon light filtering through blinds that never quite seemed to fully open. He watched the clock tick past three, the delayed bus schedule report still missing. When something took longer than expected, he was certain it meant something terrible was unfolding elsewhere. He kept the door shut, the quiet of his office a poor substitute for the stillness he craved. Even now, in a room he had occupied for fourteen years, he could not relax. His shoulders stayed drawn up, his jaw tight, as if bracing for another impact that might arrive without warning. At night, sleep offered no refuge. He would lie awake, waiting for his eyes to close, only to feel the room tilt as the memory of the collision would begin to play in his mind like a film he could not pause. The crumpled hood, the shouting of first responders, the sudden lurch of his body against the seat—it would arrive so fully that Arthur was no longer sixty-seven years old in a leather chair, but back in the wreck, certain he was trapped again. He had stopped mentioning the accident to his staff. When he scrolled past the morning news alert showing two sedans wrapped around a guardrail, his pulse jumped. He could not look away from the image of the crushed hoods, the way the vehicles had met. When his wife raised her voice across the dining room to ask if he had seen the mail, the sudden spike of sound made his chest lock. He would excuse himself, walk to the kitchen, and eat until the hollow feeling in his stomach eased, though it only returned when the quiet settled in again. Arthur kept the forced positivity separate from the dread that filled the same hour. He forced himself to think only of the good things—the students who thanked him, the garden his wife had planted, the fact that he had walked away unharmed. He was convinced the world had permanently shifted into a place where danger arrived without notice. He also wondered, with a quiet certainty, that he was permanently changed for the worse, as though something essential had fractured that day. He looked at younger men in the staff meetings and felt a sharp distance between them, a sense that somebody else would not have let the situation escalate, that somebody else would have seen the light in time. The school year had moved forward, but Arthur’s routine had contracted. He avoided going to work on days when the weather turned rough or when the superintendent’s calls seemed to stretch into silence. His assistant learned to carry her reports to his door rather than ask for his signature in person. The silence in his car was now a space he avoided entirely, taking the bus or driving only on familiar, empty roads. He did not plan to stay away from his post forever, but the weight of the delayed reports and the sudden noise of a slamming desk drawer made the office feel less like a workplace and more like a waiting room for another crash. Today, Arthur sat across from the counselor, his hands folded in his lap, the empty plate from his office lunch still nearby. He had come because the delayed emails were piling up, his wife’s concerned questions were becoming impossible to meet, and the film of the collision was starting to bleed into his morning routines. He was not sure what he expected to find here, only that he wanted to stop feeling like he was always bracing for the next impact, and that he hoped, if only for a few hours a week, to be able to sit in a quiet room without feeling the steering column buckle beneath his hands.
